evidence.quote: Capacity measures how much data fits. IOPS counts input/output operations per second. Throughput measures bytes transferred per second. I/O latency is the time one operation takes to complete.

sourceChecks.claim: Live inspected AWS comparison sections on logical numbered block addresses and independent range updates; file hierarchy is a separate interface. Diagram layer responsibilities agree.
Live inspected AWS device identification, filesystem inspection, conditional mkfs warning and mount-point instructions. Restored data must not be reformatted.

Live inspected EBS Features availability and persistence sections: replication and attachment stay within one AZ; DeleteOnTermination controls retention. These do not imply cross-zone access or deletion recovery.

Live inspected Linux fsync description, completion and directory-entry scope; followed fflush documentation for user-space versus kernel buffers. Supported durability needs appropriate buffer transfer, result handling and a scoped failure model, not transaction atomicity.

Live inspected AWS Multi-Attach limitations: ordinary XFS/EXT4 are unsuitable for concurrent servers, clustered software and application write ordering are required. Device exposure alone does not coordinate filesystems.

Live inspected EBS snapshot documentation: point-in-time written data excludes caches, creation remains pending asynchronously, and preparation must coordinate writes. Followed PostgreSQL filesystem-backup documentation for crash replay and simultaneous multi-volume requirements. Restore/retention testing is an operational requirement, not a snapshot guarantee.

Live inspected EBS I/O documentation: operation count depends on I/O size/pattern; excessive demand increases queueing latency; volume throughput and EC2 bandwidth can independently constrain performance.
Live inspected EBS volumes documentation for disk-like system/database use; AWS comparison for file/object interfaces and management costs. Database behavior remains above the volume.
